title: fusion case 10: custom ops as fusion boundaries
description:
## Scope

Case 10 of teenygrad-1bf's fusion-case taxonomy: custom ops
(`Op::Custom`/`CustomData`, backed by the `CustomOp` trait,
`core/teeny-core/src/graph/mod.rs` ~L139). Opaque by construction — no
generic body to inline, only a `name()`/`lower()` contract
(`kernels/teeny-kernels/src/graph/mod.rs`'s custom-op lowering arm, ~L2941-2947,
errors if `lower()` isn't implemented).

## Acceptance Criteria

A short written decision (this is one of the simpler cases in the taxonomy):

- Confirms custom ops are an unconditional hard fusion boundary — the
  analysis pass cannot special-case around them regardless of their
  `block()`/`grid()` shape, since there's no way to inspect or compose their
  kernel body.
- Whether a custom op can still participate as a fusion-region *boundary*
  cleanly (i.e. fusable regions on either side of it are unaffected, it's just
  never itself a fusion member) — should be yes, but state it explicitly so
  the region-identification pass in the other case subtasks doesn't need to
  special-case discovering this.

## References

Parent: teenygrad-1bf.
acceptance_criteria: Written decision confirming: (1) custom ops are an unconditional hard fusion boundary regardless of block()/grid() shape, (2) a custom op can sit at a fusion-region boundary without special-casing in other cases' region-identification passes. No code changes required.
notes:
## YOLO26 evidence (2026-08-11)

Traced the actual YOLO26n graph (vision-rs, yolo26::<f32>(80, Variant::N, OneToMany) at 64x64 input) to find concrete custom-op instances for this case. The C2PSA attention block (used twice: model.10 and model.22) produces exactly this pattern per occurrence:

  BatchNorm2d(276) -> psa_pack_qkv(277) -> flash_attention2_forward(278)  [V_hi]
                                         -> flash_attention2_forward(279)  [V_lo]
                    -> psa_extract_v_nchw(281)
  [278,279] -> psa_merge_attn_nchw(280) -> Add(284, with pe branch) -> ...

Source: crate::models::yolo::kernels::attention::psa (vision-rs), CustomOp impls
PsaPackQkvOp, PsaExtractVOp, PsaMergeAttnOp, FlashAttn2PsaOp (instantiated twice,
new_lo/new_hi). All four are genuinely opaque per this cases scope -- no unary
elementwise body to inline, real reduction/attention math inside.

This is a concrete real-world confirmation of the case-10 boundary rule: these
4 ops sit strictly between fusable regions (BatchNorm2d before, Add/Conv2d
after) and never participate as members themselves. Worth using as the
worked example when this cases decision doc gets written.

Found while investigating case-1 (teenygrad-1bf.1) pointwise op coverage against
the actual YOLO26 model in vision-rs.

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Prior art: how torch/_inductor handles this case**

Confirmed exactly as this issue's acceptance criteria assume — worth citing as validation, not new information to react to.

`ExternKernel` (`torch/_inductor/ir.py:7125`) and its `FallbackKernel` subclass (`ir.py:9477`) are the mechanism for anything inductor can't inline a generic body for. `make_fallback` (`lowering.py:2903`, dispatching on `OpOverload`/`HigherOrderOperator` at `lowering.py:2952`) is the **same registration point** used both for built-in "too hard to lower generically" ops (see the comment on teenygrad-1bf.9: sort/topk-past-the-size-limit, nonzero, unique) *and* for opaque custom ops registered via `torch.library`/higher-order ops — there's no separate code path or special-casing for "this is a user's custom op" vs. "this is a built-in op inductor chose not to lower." Both land on the identical `ExternKernelSchedulerNode`, which (per the teenygrad-1bf.9 comment) is an unconditional fusion boundary structurally — empty `get_ranges()`, `is_extern() == True` — not via any custom-op-specific check in the fusion pass.

This directly validates this issue's proposed design: teenygrad's `Op::Custom`/`CustomOp` becoming a hard fusion boundary that "the region-identification pass in the other case subtasks doesn't need to special-case discovering" is exactly inductor's shape — custom ops are just one more instance of the same generic opaque-external-kernel boundary used for every other unfusable op, not a bespoke rule. Nothing else to add; this is one of the more clear-cut cases in the taxonomy, and inductor's precedent doesn't complicate it.

title: fusion case 11: dtype-promotion boundaries
description:
## Scope

Case 11 of teenygrad-1bf's fusion-case taxonomy: dtype-promotion boundaries.
Some kernels internally upcast (e.g. an f16 op accumulating in f32 — flagged
by teenygrad-3i0/spinorml-4gx's precision notes for tensor-core paths).
Fusing two ops whose individual "public" dtype is the same but whose
*internal* precision handling differs must not silently change numerics.

## Acceptance Criteria

A written decision covering:

- A rule for when fusion is permitted across a precision boundary: either
  every member's precision contract is preserved unchanged post-fusion
  (safe default), or a fusion is rejected across a promotion boundary it
  can't prove preserves numerics.
- How this interacts with cases 1/2 (elementwise chains) specifically, since
  those are the cases most likely to actually hit mixed f16/f32-internal
  members in practice (activation functions with numerically-sensitive
  implementations, e.g. `Silu`/`Sigmoid`'s exp-based internals).
- Whether existing kernels expose enough metadata (via `RuntimeOp` or
  elsewhere) to even answer "does this op's kernel body internally promote
  precision" today, or whether that's new metadata this design needs to add.

## References

Parent: teenygrad-1bf. Related: teenygrad-3i0 (TF32/tensor-core precision
notes for the conv-epilogue case, teenygrad-1bf.8).

No code changes required.

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Prior art: how torch/_inductor handles this case**

Inductor's answer is a third option not currently on this issue's list ("preserve each member's precision contract" vs. "reject fusion it can't prove preserves numerics") — worth adding to the acceptance-criteria discussion before picking between the other two.

There is no dtype-conditioned fusion-rejection check anywhere in `scheduler.py`. The reason it's unnecessary: `upcast_compute_type` (`torch/_inductor/utils.py:4017-4025`) is applied uniformly by `DtypePropagationOpsHandler` (`dtype_propagation.py:151`) to **every individual op instruction** as the (possibly-fused) kernel body is generated — fp16/bf16 operands get promoted to fp32 for the actual compute (`config.triton.codegen_upcast_to_fp32`, on by default for the Triton backend) regardless of which "member" they originated from, and only the final store downcasts back to the buffer's declared dtype. `DtypePropagationOpsHandler.__init__` (`dtype_propagation.py:166-199`) metaprograms one promotion rule per op from `op_dtype_propagation_rules`/`pointwise_overrides_data`, applying `op_dtype_rule` -> `promote_types` (`dtype_propagation.py:203-207`) per CSE expression node.

The key structural point: dtype propagation in inductor operates at the **instruction level**, inside whatever region the scheduler already decided to fuse — it is not a property of the op/member that has to be checked for compatibility *before* fusion is allowed. A fused region's internal precision handling is *derived* from its members' instructions post-fusion, not *inherited* from each member's pre-fusion kernel body. This sidesteps the numerics-preservation proof problem this issue's acceptance criteria frame as necessary: there's no cross-member "does op A's internal upcast still happen the same way once inlined into op B's kernel" question, because upcast/downcast isn't attached to the op at all — it's attached to each instruction, applied identically whether that instruction sits in a solo kernel or a fused one.

Relevant to this issue's specific acceptance-criteria questions:
- **"A rule for when fusion is permitted across a precision boundary":** inductor's answer is "always — because precision handling is re-derived post-fusion at the instruction level, not carried over per-member," which is a stronger and simpler answer than either of this issue's two proposed options, *if* teenygrad's kernel-body generation can be restructured so precision promotion is a property of the (generated) instruction, not baked into each op's standalone kernel body ahead of time.
- **"Do existing kernels expose enough metadata to even answer 'does this op's kernel body internally promote precision' today":** inductor's model suggests the more useful question isn't "does this op internally promote" (a per-op property to query) but "is precision promotion applied as a codegen-time policy independent of which ops are present" (a property of the code generator, not the op registry) — worth considering whether teeny-kernels' kernel-body generation could adopt the same shape rather than needing new per-op metadata.
- This is most directly relevant to case 1/2 (elementwise chains, e.g. Silu/Sigmoid's exp-based internals) as this issue notes, and also to case 8's prologue-fusion boundary (dequant-into-load) per the comment posted on teenygrad-1bf.8 — worth cross-referencing that comment since it's the other case most likely to actually hit a real precision boundary in practice.

title: fusion case 12: training-mode / backward fusion
description:
## Scope

Case 12 of teenygrad-1bf's fusion-case taxonomy: training-mode / backward.
`LoweringMode::Training` (`core/teeny-core/src/model/mod.rs` ~L359) wires up
`ExecutableOp::backward_kernel_source()`/`backward_kernel_entry_point()` per
node in addition to the forward kernel.

## Acceptance Criteria

A written decision covering:

- Whether a fused-forward region either needs a coherent fused backward, or a
  per-member-composed backward (chain-rule composition of each member's
  individual backward kernel), and which of those this design targets for v1.
- Whether the analysis pass must refuse to fuse under `LoweringMode::Training`
  for regions it can't derive a backward for — and whether that refusal can
  differ per-case (e.g. case 1's plain elementwise chains are plausibly
  backward-safe via straightforward chain-rule composition; case 6's softmax-
  shaped multi-reduction almost certainly isn't for a first pass).
- Concretely which of cases 1-11 (teenygrad-1bf.1 through teenygrad-1bf.11)
  are in scope for training-mode fusion at all in v1, vs. inference-only.

## References

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Prior art: how torch/_inductor handles this case**

This directly resolves this issue's core open question ("does a fused region need a coherent fused backward, or per-member-composed backward, and which does this design target") by showing a third path that dissolves the question entirely — worth reading together with the comment on teenygrad-1bf.13, which covers the concrete backward-ABI angle of the same finding.

**Inductor itself has no special "fused-region backward" concept.** By the time Inductor ever sees a backward graph, AOTAutograd has already produced it as a plain FX graph — Inductor just runs its ordinary forward-style fusion pass (the same machinery discussed on teenygrad-1bf.1 through .9) over it a second time, with no awareness that it's "backward." There is no `backward_kernel_source()`-equivalent concept anywhere in Inductor's IR or scheduler.

The interesting decision — save-for-backward vs. recompute — happens one layer up, in `torch/_functorch/partitioners.py`'s min-cut partitioner: `min_cut_rematerialization_partition` (`partitioners.py:4109-4144`) cuts the *joint* forward+backward graph into separate fwd/bwd graphs by finding a minimum cut where "recomputable" ops are cheap to cut, so the min-cut solver prefers recomputing them in the backward rather than saving their forward output as a live activation. The recomputable-op set is a concrete literal allowlist, `default_recomputable_ops` (`partitioners.py:3163-3221` and following) — explicitly includes `aten.relu`, `aten.silu`, `aten.sigmoid`, `aten.tanh`, plus `pointwise_ops()` broadly (`partitioners.py:3295`). This is the closest ecosystem analogue to teenygrad's `is_fusable_elementwise` allowlist, but it answers a *different* question (recompute-vs-save-for-backward) than fuse-vs-not — it runs entirely before Inductor's fusion pass ever sees the graph.

Directly answers this issue's acceptance criteria:
- **"Whether a fused-forward region needs a coherent fused backward, or per-member-composed backward":** inductor's answer is **neither** — decompose each backward into ordinary forward-lowerable ops (see teenygrad-1bf.13's comment for the concrete `silu_backward` example), let the min-cut partitioner decide recompute-vs-save per op, then let the *normal* forward fusion pass (cases 1-9) fuse the resulting backward-graph ops using the exact same machinery, no special-casing.
- **"Whether the analysis pass must refuse to fuse under Training mode for regions it can't derive a backward for":** moot in inductor's model — there's no "deriving a backward for a fused region" step to refuse; every op's backward is authored once, standalone, as a decomposition (a one-time cost independent of fusion), and fusability of the resulting backward-graph ops is decided completely independently by the same rules as any forward graph.
- **"Which of cases 1-11 are in scope for training-mode fusion at all":** inductor's precedent argues this shouldn't need to be decided per-case at all if teenygrad adopts a decomposition-based backward model — every case's forward fusion machinery would automatically also apply to backward, since backward is just more forward-shaped IR by construction.

This is a materially bigger architectural swing than this issue's current scope (composing existing per-node hand-written backward kernels), so it's worth flagging as an alternative worth deciding on explicitly rather than defaulting into, given the cost of authoring hand-written backward kernels per op today (`ExecutableOp::backward_kernel_source()`) vs. authoring one decomposition per op that composes automatically.

title: fusion: x-style backward ABI for fused pointwise chains (dy,x,dx,n) -- needed for SiLU
description:
PointwiseFuse::supports_fused_backward() / is_y_style_pointwise_bwd() (pointwise_fuse.rs) only recognize the y-style backward ABI (dy, y, dx, n) used by Relu/Sigmoid/Tanh. Several real ops need a second backward ABI class -- x-style (dy, x, dx, n), which needs the original input rather than the output to compute the gradient -- and none of them can currently get a fused backward:

- **Silu** (`silu_backward` in kernels/teeny-kernels/src/nn/activation/sigmoid.rs:161, ABI confirmed by reading the kernel body: `dy_ptr, x_ptr, dx_ptr, n_elements`). This is the priority case: SiLU is the *only* elementwise activation used in the YOLO26 model (vision-rs) -- confirmed by tracing its actual graph, 87 Silu nodes, all Conv2d->BatchNorm2d->Silu triples (see the note on teenygrad-1bf.8). YOLO26 trains via yolo26_dual/Yolo26Loss::compute_grads_dual, so its Silu nodes need working backward. Whether or not case 1 (pure pointwise chains) ever fires on YOLO26 specifically (it currently does not -- no Silu-Silu adjacency exists), any future chain that *does* include a Silu member (e.g. once case 8s Conv+BN+Silu epilogue work lands and needs a fused epilogue backward) is blocked on this.
- Abs and Neg (ElemwiseAbsBackward, ElemwiseNegBackward via make_num_kernel! in graph/mod.rs) -- same x-style ABI, smaller/less urgent example.

Scope: design and implement a second backward-member class alongside the existing y-style one in lower_pointwise_fuse_backward() -- threading x (not y) through the scratch buffers for x-style members, and deciding whether/how a chain can mix y-style and x-style members (likely: only if every member is the same style, same as today, with a mixed-style chain refusing fused backward and falling back to unfused).

Not scoped to any single op batch under teenygrad-1bf.1 since it changes shared fused-backward machinery. Land after at least one op-coverage batch (teenygrad-1bf.1.2 through .7) has forward fusion working end-to-end, and validate against Silu specifically once available.

Found during an investigation into case-1 (teenygrad-1bf.1) pointwise op coverage, then confirmed as a real (not hypothetical) need by tracing the YOLO26 model graph in vision-rs.

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Prior art: how torch/_inductor handles this problem — it doesn't have it**

Checked whether inductor has an analogous fixed backward-kernel calling convention (y-style vs. x-style) for fused pointwise chains. Finding: **this problem is structurally absent in inductor**, and the reason is directly actionable for this issue.

`aten.silu_backward` is registered as a decomposition, not a hand-written kernel (`torch/_decomp/decompositions.py:302-307`):

```python
@register_decomposition(aten.silu_backward)
def silu_backward(grad_output, self):
    sigmoid = torch.sigmoid(self)
    return grad_output * sigmoid * (1 + self * (1 - sigmoid))
```

This is exactly teenygrad's "x-style" formula — it uses `self` (the original input `x`), not `y` (silu's output) — but in inductor it is never a monolithic kernel with a fixed `(dy, x, dx, n)` (or `(dy, y, dx, n)`) calling convention at all. It's ordinary tensor arithmetic that gets traced into the joint graph as four or five plain aten nodes (`sigmoid`, `mul`, `sub`, `add`, `mul`). Each of those nodes is then independently either recomputed or saved by the min-cut partitioner (`aten.sigmoid`/`aten.silu` are both in `default_recomputable_ops`, `torch/_functorch/partitioners.py:3193,3217` — see the comment on teenygrad-1bf.12 for the full mechanism), and the resulting ops simply flow through the **exact same** pointwise-fusion machinery as any forward elementwise chain (the `numel==numel, rnumel==rnumel` check discussed on teenygrad-1bf.1) — no separate "backward ABI" layer exists to design, and no y-style/x-style distinction needs tracking anywhere, because there's no fixed-signature backward kernel body for a style to be a property *of*.

**This is the sharpest structural difference found across the whole taxonomy**, worth flagging explicitly rather than folding quietly into the case-12 comment: teenygrad's `ExecutableOp::backward_kernel_source()` model requires every op to ship a hand-written backward kernel with a fixed calling convention that a fusion pass must then thread scratch buffers through (which is exactly what's blocking Silu today, per this issue). Inductor's model instead requires every backward to be expressible as a **decomposition into existing forward-lowerable ops** — so there is never a bespoke backward-kernel-body or ABI to compose. The "which ABI does this op use" question dissolves into "is this decomposition already correct forward-op math," which is a one-time authoring cost per op (write `x * sigmoid(x) * (1 + x*(1-sigmoid(x)))` once, using ops that already exist) rather than a per-fusion-case ABI-compatibility problem that recurs for every new op needing fused backward (as this issue's own Abs/Neg examples show happening again).

Concretely for this issue's stated scope: rather than adding a second backward-member class (x-style) alongside the existing y-style one in `lower_pointwise_fuse_backward()`, it may be worth asking whether Silu/Abs/Neg's backward can instead be expressed as a **decomposition into ops teeny-kernels can already forward-fuse** (Silu backward needs `sigmoid`, `mul`, `sub`, `add` — all presumably already fusable-elementwise per case 1's allowlist) — which would let case 1's existing forward-fusion machinery handle it "for free," the same way inductor's does, instead of building and maintaining a second backward-ABI class that will need a third/fourth class for the next op that doesn't fit either shape. This is a bigger swing than this issue's current scope (which explicitly targets extending `lower_pointwise_fuse_backward()`), so worth an explicit decision rather than defaulting into the narrower fix, especially since this issue already anticipates "any future chain that does include a Silu member... is blocked on this" recurring.

title: fusion taxonomy: windowed-reduction pooling ops (MaxPool2d etc.) don't map to any of the 12 cases
description:
None of teenygrad-1bf1 through .12 clearly covers pooling ops (MaxPool1d/2d/3d, AvgPool*, LpPool*, GlobalAvgPool, GlobalMaxPool). They are windowed reductions -- structurally closer to case 4 (reduction-terminated regions) than to elementwise, but case 4s text is written around a single reduction op terminating an elementwise chain, not a standalone windowed/strided reduction with its own tiling.

Concrete evidence this is not just a hypothetical gap: traced the actual YOLO26n graph (vision-rs) -- SPPF (blocks/sppf.rs) chains 3 MaxPool2d nodes directly back-to-back (graph nodes 116->117->118, each consuming the previous, kernel_h=kernel_w=5, stride=1) before a ChannelCat. That is a same-op reduction chain with a real fusion opportunity (3 launches -> fewer), and it does not fit case 1 (not elementwise), case 4 (not reduction-terminating an elementwise chain, and not a single reduction), or any other existing case.

Separately (smaller, related): the same trace found 2 places where Silu feeds directly into UpsampleNearest2d (graph nodes 151->152 and 186->187) with no elementwise chain in between -- an elementwise-into-reindex adjacency that sits right on the boundary between case 1 and case 7 (free reindex ops) and is not clearly assigned to either.

Scope: a written decision (same style as the other case docs) on whether pooling gets its own case (13?) or folds into case 4s scope with that case broadened, plus a explicit ruling on the elementwise->reindex boundary noted above.

Found while investigating case-1 (teenygrad-1bf.1) pointwise op coverage against the actual YOLO26 model in vision-rs.
close_reason: Decision recorded: pooling stays its own case (not folded into case 4/teenygrad-1bf.4) — validated against both torch/_inductor's NestedReduction (explicitly excludes same-size/output-size-reducing dependent reductions) and TensorRT/Myelin's separate 'dedicated kernels' bucket for pooling. Elementwise->reindex boundary (Silu->UpsampleNearest2d) ruled not a new case, covered once cases 1/7 share a fusion mechanism. Full reasoning in comments.
