comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Prior art: how torch/_inductor handles this case**

Inductor's answer is that overlapping-window pooling is a non-problem for its fusion model specifically *because* it never materializes or shares window reads between output elements — worth citing since it reframes this issue's "doesn't fit any case because one input element is read by multiple output windows" concern as a non-issue for a recompute-oriented fusion model (see also the fan-out/case-3 comment on teenygrad-1bf.3, which covers the same materialize-vs-recompute tradeoff).

- Inductor lowers max-pool as an ordinary `Reduction` IR node with a custom, overlap-aware index function — no special "windowed reduction" IR variant exists. `_max_pool_with_offsets` (`torch/_inductor/lowering.py:5783-5855`) sets `ranges=new_size` (pooled *output* spatial shape) and `reduction_ranges=kernel_size` (the pooling window), with `inner_fn=fn_inner` (`lowering.py:5819-5826`): given an output index `idx` and a reduction index `reduction_idx` (position within the window), it computes the input index as `bh[i]*stride[i] + reduction_idx[i]*dilation[i] - padding[i]` and loads from there. Overlap between adjacent output windows is handled purely by this per-output-element index arithmetic re-deriving overlapping input reads on demand — not by any special-cased overlap-aware structure or shared intermediate buffer.
- The reduction itself is just `Reduction.create(reduction_type="max", ...)` (`lowering.py:5828-5837`) — the exact same IR class used for sum/mean/etc. elsewhere (same class discussed for case 4/5, teenygrad-1bf.4/.5).
- Out-of-bounds reads (padding/dilation/ceil_mode) go through `constant_boundary_condition(x, min_value, dim=n_dim)` (`lowering.py:5814-5815`), not the index function.
- `argmax` for the indices output is computed the same way (`lowering.py:5838-5847`).
- Because it's an unremarkable `Reduction` node, it fuses with neighboring elementwise producers/consumers via the exact same generic scheduler machinery as any other reduction — **no fusability special-casing exists for pooling at all** in inductor.

Directly relevant to this issue's framing: this suggests pooling doesn't need its own new case in the taxonomy any more than it needs one in inductor — it can fold into case 4's scope (teenygrad-1bf.4, reduction-terminated regions) as long as case 4's design allows the reduction's index function to be "windowed" (parameterized by kernel_size/stride/dilation/padding rather than spanning the whole axis) rather than assuming the reduction always covers its full input dimension. The three-MaxPool2d-in-a-row SPPF chain this issue found (nodes 116->117->118) would then be case-4-style reduction/reduction fusion (also covered structurally by `SIMDScheduling.can_fuse`'s reduction/reduction path in inductor, per the teenygrad-1bf.4 comment) rather than needing a distinct mechanism.

On the separate Silu->UpsampleNearest2d boundary question this issue raises: inductor's `View`/`ReinterpretView`/upsample-as-index-math handling (see the case-7 comment, once posted on teenygrad-1bf.7) draws that line based on whether the op changes strides/offsets only vs. needs its own compute — worth checking that comment once available for how inductor would classify an elementwise-into-reindex adjacency like this.

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Correction to my earlier comment on this issue, re: the SPPF MaxPool2d chain specifically**

My previous comment claimed the 3-node MaxPool2d chain (nodes 116->117->118, `kernel_h=kernel_w=5, stride=1`) "would be case-4-style reduction/reduction fusion, also covered structurally by `SIMDScheduling.can_fuse`'s reduction/reduction path." That was wrong — I hadn't actually traced the reduction/reduction branch of that function when I wrote it. Having now read it directly: **inductor would not fuse this chain into one kernel either.** Correcting the record, because the real answer is more useful to this issue's decision than what I said before.

**The generic path can't handle reduction-feeds-reduction at all.** `SIMDScheduling.can_fuse` (`torch/_inductor/codegen/simd.py`) has exactly three branches: both-pointwise (`simd.py:2141`), pointwise-producer-into-reduction (`simd.py:2205`, asserts `rnumel1 == 1` — i.e. the producer must *not* itself be a reduction), and reduction-producer-into-pointwise (handled by swapping args to hit the second branch, `simd.py:2242`). There is no fourth branch for reduction-into-reduction: the fallthrough at `simd.py:2237-2240` (`if not node1.is_reduction() or node2.is_reduction(): raise AssertionError(...)`) means if this function is ever reached with *both* nodes being reductions, it raises rather than deciding — this code path is written on the assumption that a reduction/reduction pair never reaches it.

**There is a dedicated mechanism for dependent reduction pairs — but it's deliberately narrow, and excludes this exact shape.** `NestedReduction`/`FusedNestedReductions` (`scheduler.py:518`, `scheduler.py:3088`) exists specifically to fuse "an outer reduction and a dependent grouped reduction... into one kernel." But per its own docstring (`scheduler.py:527-530`): "This is deliberately limited to same-total-numel pairs: both reductions must traverse the same number of logical elements. **General output-size-reducing nested reductions, including split reductions, need different grid ownership and are rejected here.**" Its worked example is "layernorm + block amax" — a big reduction (e.g. rnumel=768 over a full row) plus a smaller *sub-group* reduction over the same elements (e.g. rnumel=32 amax-per-32-chunk) — a hierarchical big/small split, not a chain of independently-sized windowed poolings.

Concretely, `NestedReduction.can_fuse` (`scheduler.py:864-885`) requires the two reductions' sizes to differ: `if V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(outer_rnumel, grouped_rnumel): return False` (`scheduler.py:884-885`). SPPF's three `MaxPool2d` nodes all use the *same* kernel size (`kernel_h=kernel_w=5` -> `rnumel=25` for every one of them), so this check would reject every adjacent pair in that chain — `NestedReduction` was built for "one big reduction, one small nested one," not "N reductions of identical size chained back to back."

**Net finding:** inductor hits the same wall this issue found. A same-size windowed-reduction chain (three stride-1 MaxPool2d in a row, SPPF-style) doesn't fit inductor's generic fusion path (structurally can't handle reduction/reduction at all) *or* its dedicated nested-reduction mechanism (explicitly scoped to differently-sized, non-output-size-reducing pairs). This is genuinely useful, different from what my earlier comment implied: it's not that teenygrad is missing a trick a mature compiler already has — it's that even a mature, heavily-optimized production compiler treats this as a case worth a dedicated, narrowly-scoped mechanism (`NestedReduction`) rather than folding it into the generic path, and that mechanism's own docstring explicitly carves out "output-size-reducing" chains (which is what overlapping-window pooling is) as **out of scope**, needing "different grid ownership."

That's a concrete, useful signal for this issue's acceptance criteria ("whether pooling gets its own case (13?) or folds into case 4's scope"): inductor's precedent argues for **not** folding same-size windowed-reduction chains into case 4's mechanism, since even inductor's team drew that exact boundary deliberately (a dedicated nested-reduction class, explicitly excluding the pooling-chain shape) rather than generalizing case 4's producer-into-reduction check to cover it. If this design does eventually want to fuse chains like SPPF's, `NestedReduction`'s docstring reasoning ("different grid ownership") is the right starting citation for *why* it's hard, not just *that* it's hard: each pooling stage in the chain wants CTA/grid ownership sized to its own window, and a chain of them doesn't have one authoritative shape the way case 4's reduction-terminated-elementwise-chain does (single reduction, unambiguous grid owner).

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Additional info: TensorRT also keeps pooling out of its general fusion mechanism, per vision-rs's TensorRT analysis**

Full writeup posted as a comment on the parent (teenygrad-1bf); the specific finding for this issue, and a second independent data point supporting the correction I posted above (re: inductor's `NestedReduction` mechanism not covering the SPPF chain shape either).

`spinorml-1fj` (vision-rs)'s headline kernel-time breakdown for YOLO26n on TensorRT has **"Depthwise conv / pooling (dedicated kernels)" as its own category (2.9% of GPU time), entirely separate from "Myelin JIT-fused kernels" (25.7%)**. TensorRT does not route pooling through Myelin's general arbitrary-op-chain fusion mechanism at all — it uses separate, presumably vendor-hand-optimized dedicated kernels for pooling instead. This wasn't previously called out anywhere in this issue or the parent spec's citations of `spinorml-1fj`.

Combined with the `torch/_inductor` finding already posted here (inductor's dedicated dependent-reduction-fusion mechanism, `NestedReduction`, explicitly excludes "output-size-reducing" reductions like pooling and requires the two reductions to have *different* sizes — SPPF's same-kernel-size chain doesn't qualify): **two independent production systems (TensorRT/Myelin and torch/_inductor) both keep windowed/pooling reductions structurally separate from their general elementwise/reduction op-fusion machinery**, rather than folding pooling into the same mechanism that handles arbitrary elementwise+reduction chains. Neither treats "chain of same-size windowed reductions" (the SPPF case) as something their general fusion pass attempts.

This is a meaningfully stronger signal for this issue's "does pooling get its own case, or fold into case 4" decision than I had when I posted the case-4-folding suggestion below: the empirical pattern across both reference systems is that pooling is handled by its *own* dedicated mechanism/kernels, separate from the general reduction-fusion path — not because pooling can't be `Reduction`-shaped (both systems do lower it as an ordinary reduction with a custom index function for windowing, per the inductor `_max_pool_with_offsets` mechanism already documented here), but because chaining multiple pooling stages together for fusion purposes is apparently not worth either compiler team's effort to generalize their reduction-fusion path to cover, or runs into the same "different grid ownership" problem inductor's `NestedReduction` docstring flags. Worth treating "pooling stays its own case, dedicated mechanism, likely deferred/hand-written rather than folded into case 4's generalized retiling" as the leading candidate for this issue's written decision, rather than a 50/50 toss-up between the two options.

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Decision**

Closing with the following written decision, per this issue's acceptance criteria.

**1. Pooling (MaxPool1d/2d/3d, AvgPool*, LpPool*, GlobalAvgPool, GlobalMaxPool): stays its own case, does not fold into case 4 (teenygrad-1bf.4).**

Reasoning, based on prior-art research from both reference fusion compilers examined in this tracker:

- **torch/_inductor**: has a dedicated mechanism for fusing dependent reduction pairs, `NestedReduction`/`FusedNestedReductions` (`torch/_inductor/scheduler.py:518`, `:3088`) — but its own docstring explicitly scopes it to *same-total-numel, differently-sized* nested reductions (its worked example: layernorm + block-amax) and states "General output-size-reducing nested reductions, including split reductions, need different grid ownership and are rejected here." The concrete gate (`scheduler.py:884-885`) requires the two reductions' sizes to differ (`rnumel1 != rnumel2`). SPPF's three chained `MaxPool2d` nodes share the same kernel size (`rnumel=25` for all three), so they'd fail this gate — inductor would not fuse this chain even with its dedicated nested-reduction mechanism. (See the correction comment above for the full trace confirming inductor's *generic* fusion path can't handle reduction-into-reduction at all — it hits a bare `raise AssertionError` in that branch.)
- **TensorRT/Myelin**: the nsys-profiled kernel-time breakdown for YOLO26n (`spinorml-1fj`, vision-rs) has "Depthwise conv / pooling (dedicated kernels)" as its own category (2.9%), entirely separate from "Myelin JIT-fused kernels" (25.7%). TensorRT does not route pooling through its general arbitrary-op-chain fusion mechanism at all.

Two independent, mature production fusion compilers both keep windowed/pooling reductions structurally separate from their general elementwise+reduction fusion machinery, rather than generalizing that machinery to cover same-size dependent-reduction chains. Both still lower pooling as an ordinary `Reduction`-shaped op internally (inductor's `_max_pool_with_offsets`, `lowering.py:5783-5855`, uses a custom overlap-aware index function over a plain `Reduction` node — no special "windowed reduction" IR variant) — the gap is specifically in *fusing multiple such reductions together*, not in representing one.

**v1 scope for teenygrad**: pooling gets its own case (distinct from case 4), and same-size back-to-back pooling chains (the SPPF shape) are **out of v1 scope** — treat each pooling op as its own kernel launch, same as inductor and TensorRT both do today. If this is revisited later, `NestedReduction`'s docstring reasoning ("different grid ownership") is the right starting point for *why* it's hard: each stage in a pooling chain wants CTA/grid ownership sized to its own window, and unlike case 4 (single reduction, one unambiguous grid owner), a chain of same-size poolings has no single authoritative shape to retile around.

**2. Elementwise-into-reindex boundary (Silu -> UpsampleNearest2d): not a new case — covered once cases 1 and 7 share a fusion mechanism.**

`UpsampleNearest2d` is pure index arithmetic (each output pixel maps to its nearest input pixel via address computation, no compute) — structurally identical in kind to reshape/slice/concat, i.e. squarely case 7's (teenygrad-1bf.7) "free reindex ops" scope, not a new op class. `Silu` is case 1's (teenygrad-1bf.1) scope. Both share the same uniform, flat elementwise/index-arithmetic CTA structure (no reduction, no retiling needed) — per the parent issue's cross-cutting notes (and the inductor/TensorRT research posted throughout this tracker), cases 1, 2, 3, 5, and 7 are all candidates to collapse into one generalized "same-CTA-shape, DAG-region" fusion mechanism rather than needing per-pair-of-cases boundary rules. Under that framing, "elementwise producer feeding a free-reindex consumer" isn't a boundary between two mechanisms that needs its own ruling — it's a single region that mechanism should already handle, the same way it'd handle Silu feeding another Silu or a reshape feeding a Silu. No dedicated ruling needed beyond confirming this adjacency is in-scope for whichever unified mechanism cases 1/7 end up sharing.

**Net**: this issue found a real, non-hypothetical gap (validated as a real gap in two independent production compilers, not just teenygrad's own taxonomy) for pooling-chain fusion, correctly scoped it out of v1, and found the second concern (elementwise->reindex adjacency) was not actually a gap once cases 1 and 7 are read as sharing a mechanism rather than being fully independent.

title: fusion case 2: multi-input elementwise / fan-in (broadcast, residual-add)
description:
## Scope

Case 2 of teenygrad-1bf's fusion-case taxonomy: multi-input elementwise /
fan-in (broadcast, residual-add). E.g. `x + f(x)`, bias-add, a two-branch
elementwise merge — two producers feeding one elementwise consumer.

`Graph::fuse_elementwise_chains()` (`core/teeny-core/src/graph/mod.rs` ~L1856)
today assumes a *linear chain* with exactly one consumer per interior node.
This case needs a DAG region (multiple producers, one consumer node), which
that pass's eligibility check does not currently express.

## Acceptance Criteria

A written decision covering:

- How region *identification* generalizes from "adjacent single-consumer
  chain" to "DAG region with bounded fan-in" — what bounds fan-in (e.g. must
  all producers themselves be fusable-elementwise, or can one be an arbitrary
  external tensor?).
- How broadcast shape mismatches between operands feeding the same fused
  iteration domain are handled (different rank/strides) — does the fused
  kernel's index arithmetic need per-operand broadcast maps (cf. the
  Hexagon-MLIR paper's per-operand affine indexing maps `φ_ℓ`, cited in the
  parent spec), or is this deferred to only same-shape operands for v1?
- Whether this case's `Op` representation is still `Op::Fused`'s member-list
  shape or needs a richer subgraph representation (the parent spec's
  "Representation" open question) — this is likely the first case where a
  linear `Vec<Op>` chain genuinely isn't expressive enough.

## References

Parent: teenygrad-1bf.
acceptance_criteria: Written decision on: (1) how region identification generalizes from linear-chain to bounded-fan-in DAG region, (2) how broadcast shape mismatches between operands are handled in the fused iteration domain, (3) whether Op::Fused's Vec<Op> shape suffices or a richer subgraph representation is needed. No code changes required.
delete_reason: superseded: re-created with Anduin + Tile/shared-memory composition design (teenygrad-3w0 follow-on)

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Prior art: how torch/_inductor handles this case**

Notably, this case isn't a special case in inductor at all — it falls out for free of the same machinery as case 1 (see comment on teenygrad-1bf.1), because `SchedulerNode` was never chain-shaped to begin with.

- `x + f(x)` (or any multi-input elementwise op) is just an `ir.Pointwise` whose `inner_fn` loads from however many operand buffers it needs. Broadcasting between differently-shaped operands is resolved at **IR-construction time** in `lowering.py` (via the pointwise-op builder's shape broadcasting), not in the scheduler — so by the time a `SchedulerNode` exists, every operand read is already expressed as an index formula over one common iteration domain. There's no separate "reconcile broadcast shapes across fused members" step because it never becomes a cross-member problem; it's resolved once, at IR build time, same as for an unfused op.
- Dependency extraction (`torch/_inductor/dependencies.py`) pulls an **arbitrary-arity** `reads` set straight from `inner_fn` — not a fixed arity of 1.
- `Scheduler.can_fuse_vertical` (`scheduler.py:8469`) fuses a producer into a consumer by checking that the consumer's `unmet_dependencies` are each satisfied by a producer write or an already-scheduled node — it iterates over however many reads the consumer has.
- Horizontal fusion (two independent nodes sharing a common ancestor — e.g. two branches of a fan-in both reading `x`) reuses the *same* function: `V.choices.can_fuse_horizontal` aliases to `can_fuse` (`torch/_inductor/codegen/simd.py:2264`).

Relevant to this issue's open questions:
- **Region identification "linear chain vs. DAG region":** inductor never had a linear-chain-only representation to generalize away from — every `SchedulerNode`/`FusedSchedulerNode` is already a DAG-region concept, with dependency edges tracked per-buffer, not per-adjacent-pair. If this design ends up needing to support fan-in generally (not just for this one case), that argues for generalizing `Op::Fused`'s representation once, rather than case-by-case — inductor's approach suggests the DAG-region representation is not actually harder to reason about than the chain one, since fusability there is still just "read/write dependency graph plus shape/tiling compatibility," independent of topology.
- **Broadcast/differing-shape operands:** inductor's answer is "resolved before scheduling ever sees it, not during fusion" — worth considering whether teenygrad's fused-region eligibility check should similarly defer to whatever already reconciles broadcast shapes for un-fused multi-input ops today, rather than inventing new per-operand broadcast maps specifically for the fused case.

title: fusion case 3: fan-out — value consumed by multiple downstream ops
description:
## Scope

Case 3 of teenygrad-1bf's fusion-case taxonomy: fan-out — a value consumed by
multiple downstream ops. Fusion can't simply inline-and-discard the producer;
it must choose materialize-once (write to memory, multiple readers) vs.
recompute-per-consumer (duplicate the producing op's work inside each fused
branch).

The Hexagon-MLIR paper (arXiv:2602.19762, cited in the parent spec) explicitly
flags "re-computations" as a fusion-correctness/cost concern for exactly this
shape.

## Acceptance Criteria

A written decision covering:

- The cost model for choosing materialize vs. recompute: cheap-to-recompute
  ops (e.g. a single elementwise activation) vs. expensive ones (e.g. a
  reduction feeding two consumers) likely want different defaults.
- How the region-identification pass (case 2) is expected to *detect* fan-out
  at all — does it walk consumer counts per graph node the way
  `fuse_elementwise_chains`'s existing single-consumer check already does (just
  inverted to allow it under a rule, instead of unconditionally blocking it)?
- Whether fan-out is in v1 scope at all, or explicitly deferred (materialize
  always, i.e. never fuse across a multi-consumer node) as the simplest
  correct-by-construction starting point.

## References

Parent: teenygrad-1bf. Related: case 2 (teenygrad-1bf.2) — fan-out is the
inverse-shaped problem to fan-in and likely shares region-identification
machinery with it.
acceptance_criteria: Written decision on: (1) the materialize-vs-recompute cost model for a value with multiple consumers, (2) how fan-out is detected during region identification, (3) whether fan-out is in v1 scope or explicitly deferred (always materialize). No code changes required.
delete_reason: superseded: re-created with Anduin + Tile/shared-memory composition design (teenygrad-3w0 follow-on)

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Prior art: how torch/_inductor handles this case**

This directly answers the issue's framing ("must be a deliberate cost-model decision... not silently defaulted either way") — inductor *does* default silently, but to a specific, documented rule, which is itself useful prior art for what "the simplest correct-by-construction starting point" could look like if this design wants one.

Inductor makes this decision at **lowering time**, before a `Scheduler` even exists (earlier than case 1/2's decision point):

- Right after each FX node is lowered, `GraphLowering.run_node` calls `result.mark_reuse(len(n.users))` (`torch/_inductor/graph.py:2239`) — `len(n.users)` is the fan-out count read straight off the FX graph.
- `mark_reuse` (`ir.py:875`, `ir.py:3551`, and `ir.py:10858` for `StorageBox`) calls `should_realize_on_reuse` (`ir.py:10823-10855`) — this is the actual cost model, and its **default is recompute-per-consumer** (leave the producer inlined, let each consumer's kernel re-execute the producing `inner_fn`), *unless* one of a small number of explicit heuristics trips:
  - uses `inline_asm_elementwise` -> always realize
  - on CPU, op is in a hardcoded "heavy_ops" list (exp/log/log10/log1p/log2/sigmoid/tanh) -> realize, because recomputing something exp-based per consumer is a bad trade
  - `has_large_inner_fn()` -> realize
  - `graph_reuse and self.num_reads() > config.realize_reads_threshold`, where `realize_reads_threshold = 4` (`torch/_inductor/config.py:908`) -> realize
- When none of those trip, `self.realize()` is *not* called and the value stays inlined — recomputed inside every consumer's kernel.

So inductor's shipped answer to "materialize vs. recompute" is: **recompute by default, materialize only on a handful of cheap heuristic trip-wires** (a short expensive-op-name list + a read-count threshold), not a general cost model weighing recompute-cost against consumer-count. This is a reasonable reference point if this issue's acceptance criteria end up favoring "materialize always" as the v1 starting point instead — inductor demonstrates that the *other* default (recompute-by-default) also ships fine in practice, provided you carve out a small number of "this is definitely not worth recomputing" exceptions rather than trying to build a real cost model up front.

Detection: same as case 2, this is naturally exposed by inductor's per-buffer user-count (`len(n.users)` from the FX graph) rather than a bespoke consumer-count walk — if this design's region-identification pass already tracks per-node consumer counts for other reasons (e.g. case 2's fan-in), case 3's fan-out detection is the same data read the other direction.

title: fusion case 4: reduction-terminated regions
description:
## Scope

Case 4 of teenygrad-1bf's fusion-case taxonomy: reduction-terminated regions
— elementwise producer(s) feeding a single reduction (`Op::ReduceSum`,
`ReduceMax`, `ReduceMean`, `ReduceProd`, `ReduceL1`, `ReduceL2`,
`ReduceLogSum`, `ReduceLogSumExp`, `ReduceSumSquare`, all already itemized in
`core/teeny-core/src/graph/mod.rs`'s `Op` enum).

Per spinorml-1fj's Myelin nsys data (vision-rs beads project), a reduction
forces ONE CTA/thread structure for the *entire* fused region, not just the
reduction op itself — e.g. `__myl_MulMaxrSubExpSum` runs at `block=(32,4,1)`
(warp-per-row), with all surrounding elementwise ops running under that shape
rather than their own natural 256-wide one. This is exactly spinorml-1fj.2's
open "retiling" problem.

## Acceptance Criteria

A written decision covering:

- Concretely: given N member ops with differing "natural" `block()`/`grid()`,
  how is the winning shape chosen (empirically: most-demanding member —
  reduction beats elementwise), and how do the losing members' per-thread
  index arithmetic get re-derived under it?
- Whether this subtask absorbs a concrete answer from spinorml-1fj.2 (if
  resolved by the time this is picked up) or explicitly scopes retiling out of
  v1 and restricts fusion to already-same-shape regions only, treating any
  region containing a reduction as unfused until the retiling design lands.
- How the fused `RuntimeOp`'s `block()`/`grid()` are synthesized when they
  can no longer just delegate to one member (unlike case 1) — this is the
  first case where that delegation shortcut breaks.

## References

Parent: teenygrad-1bf. Prior art: spinorml-1fj.2 (vision-rs beads project) —
investigates the retiling algorithm itself; this subtask should either cite a
resolution there or explicitly punt.
acceptance_criteria: Written decision on: (1) how the winning CTA/thread shape is chosen among members with differing natural block()/grid(), (2) how losing members' index arithmetic is re-derived under it (or an explicit citation to spinorml-1fj.2's resolution), (3) how the fused RuntimeOp's block()/grid() are synthesized when they can no longer delegate to one member. No code changes required.
delete_reason: superseded: re-created with Anduin + Tile/shared-memory composition design (teenygrad-3w0 follow-on)

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Prior art: how torch/_inductor handles this case**

Inductor's answer to the "N members, differing natural block()/grid(), who wins" question is: the reduction wins by construction, via a tiling-compatibility check performed at the same point as case 1's shape check, not a separate retiling pass.

Same unified function as case 1: `SIMDScheduling.can_fuse` handles pointwise/pointwise, pointwise/reduction, *and* reduction/reduction pairs (`can_fuse_vertical = can_fuse_horizontal = can_fuse`, `torch/_inductor/codegen/simd.py:2264-2265`). For a non-reduction producer feeding a reduction consumer (`simd.py:2201-2231`):

- Asserts `rnumel1 == 1` (the producer's own domain has no reduction dim).
- Requires `numel1 == numel2 * rnumel2` — the producer's total element count must exactly equal the reduction's *input* footprint (batch dim x reduced dim).
- If that holds, `SIMDKernel.is_compatible((numel2, rnumel2), n.get_ranges())` (`simd.py:2205-2209`) checks every member's index ranges actually tile against the reduction's `(numel2, rnumel2)` domain.
- When `config.triton.tiling_prevents_reduction_fusion` is set, the producer's allowed tiling is further restricted to one of two shapes: `(numel1, 1)` or `(numel2, rnumel2, 1)` (`simd.py:2210-2216`).

That restriction *is* the retiling decision: the reduction's shape is authoritative, and a pointwise producer is only allowed to fuse if its own natural tiling collapses into the reduction's tiling — never the other way around. This directly matches this issue's empirical finding (reduction beats elementwise) and gives it a concrete mechanical form: not "choose the most demanding member's shape and re-derive everyone else's index math," but "reject fusion unless the pointwise member's tiling is already expressible as a sub-tiling of the reduction's domain" — i.e. inductor never actually re-derives index arithmetic for a shape mismatch; it just refuses to fuse across one it can't cleanly express. Worth citing as a candidate answer for this issue's "how do losing members' per-thread index arithmetic get re-derived" question: the shipped answer in inductor's codebase is "they don't get re-derived; fusion is instead gated on the shapes already being compatible via a numel-equality + tiling-subset check."

The *concrete* launch config (block size, persistent-vs-looped reduction) is decided separately, later, per already-fused kernel, during codegen — not part of the fusability decision above: `TritonKernel.should_use_persistent_reduction` (`torch/_inductor/codegen/triton.py:3759`) delegates to `V.choices.should_use_persistent_reduction(features, cooperative_reduction)`, using `ReductionHint` (`torch/_inductor/runtime/hints.py:50`: `INNER`/`OUTER`/`OUTER_TINY`/`DEFAULT`) to pick whether the fused region's reduction axis is materialized in registers (persistent) or looped.

This also bears on the parent spec's "when is fusion decided" open question: inductor cleanly separates (1) iteration-domain/legality — decided during the scheduler fusion pass using only symbolic `numel`/`rnumel`/tiling signatures that exist immediately after lowering (no concrete GPU launch parameters needed, since shapes are known from trace time) — from (2) concrete launch config — decided per already-fused kernel, later, during codegen/autotuning. Suggests this design's answer should lean toward option (b): decouple the fusability *decision* (symbolic shape/tiling comparison, cheap and available right after `Graph::optimise()`) from `block()`/`grid()` *materialization* (done once per fused region, at `TritonLowering` time) — rather than requiring concrete `RuntimeOp::block()/grid()` values to exist before fusion can even be evaluated.

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Additional info: the empirical basis for "retiling is a real, distinct transformation," per vision-rs's TensorRT analysis**

Full writeup posted as a comment on the parent (teenygrad-1bf); summarizing what's directly relevant here.

`spinorml-1fj` (vision-rs) profiled TensorRT's actual generated kernels and confirmed the retiling problem this case describes is real, not a theoretical worry: `__myl_MulMaxrSubExpSum` (softmax-shaped: Mul->Max->Sub->Exp->Sum) runs at `block=(32,4,1)` (warp-per-row) with 64B dynamic shared memory — a genuinely different structure than the `block=(256,1,1)` used by every purely-elementwise `__myl_*` kernel in the same trace. Myelin doesn't stitch per-op phases together with internal barriers; it picks one CTA/thread scheme up front, driven by the single most constraining op (the reduction), and reformulates *everything else* in the chain around it.

More useful for this issue's decision than the "reduction wins" headline: `spinorml-1fj`'s follow-up comment reasons through *why* this can't be achieved by simple kernel-source concatenation, which bears directly on "how do losing members' per-thread index arithmetic get re-derived":
> "A kernel launch has ONE fixed grid/block shape for its entire body. Concatenation doesn't reconcile two kernels' differing natural thread mappings — it just picks whichever launch config the fused kernel actually runs with, and the other kernel's indexing math (written assuming its own original config) is now wrong under it... Inlining/DCE don't retile — they don't re-derive per-thread work assignment when the physical thread layout changes. This retiling is exactly what Myelin's fusion actually does... a bespoke transformation per fusion, not a generic optimizer pass."

I.e. vision-rs's own conclusion (independently, before this taxonomy was written) is that retiling is a genuine, separate mechanism that has to be designed, not something that falls out of extending case 1's (teenygrad-1bf.1) concatenation approach with more bookkeeping. Worth citing directly in this issue's decision doc as corroboration for scoping retiling out of v1 (per this issue's own acceptance criteria's stated fallback) rather than attempting a lightweight version of it.

Also worth noting for the "unrestricted" end of this case: the same trace has an 11-op mega-fusion, `__myl_ConcSigmAddSubConcMulConcTranSlicMaxrReshSlic` (Concat->Sigmoid->Add->Sub->Concat->Mul->Concat->Transpose->Slice->Max->Reshape->Slice — almost certainly YOLO26's detection-head decode/NMS-prep step), which runs under the *same* `block=(32,4,1)`/64B-shared-mem structure as the simple softmax kernel above — i.e. once retiling is solved for one reduction-anchored chain, it generalizes to arbitrarily long surrounding elementwise/reindex chains for free, not just short ones. Useful evidence that if/when retiling is tackled, it's worth designing for arbitrary chain length from the start rather than a narrow "reduction plus one or two elementwise ops" case.

title: fusion case 5: reduction with elementwise epilogue (RMSNorm-shaped)
description:
## Scope

Case 5 of teenygrad-1bf's fusion-case taxonomy: reduction with an elementwise
epilogue — RMSNorm-shaped (reduce sum-of-squares → rsqrt → elementwise
divide+scale). The reduction is not the last op in the region; downstream
elementwise ops consume the *reduced* scalar/vector alongside the original
input tensor. Distinct from case 4 (teenygrad-1bf.4) in data-flow shape: one
input feeds both the reduction and, later, the epilogue directly (not just
the reduction's own output feeding forward).

## Acceptance Criteria

A written decision covering:

- How the region-identification pass recognizes this two-role-input shape
  (same tensor feeding both the reduction branch and the epilogue branch)
  distinctly from case 2's fan-in and case 4's reduction-terminated shape.
- Whether the retiling answer from case 4 (teenygrad-1bf.4) — reduction drives
  the CTA/thread shape for the whole region — applies unchanged here, or needs
  adjustment because the epilogue also directly reads the pre-reduction input
  (not just the reduction's scalar output).
- Existing hand-written `RmsNormForward` kernel
  (`kernels/teeny-kernels/src/.../norm/rmsnorm.rs`) as the reference
  implementation a generated version must match numerically and
  performance-wise.

## References

Parent: teenygrad-1bf. Related: teenygrad-1bf.4 (reduction-terminated
regions) — likely shares the retiling mechanism once that's resolved.
acceptance_criteria: Written decision on: (1) how the region-identification pass recognizes the two-role-input shape (same tensor feeding both reduction and epilogue), (2) whether case 4's retiling answer applies unchanged, (3) confirms RmsNormForward as the correctness/perf reference. No code changes required.
delete_reason: superseded: re-created with Anduin + Tile/shared-memory composition design (teenygrad-3w0 follow-on)

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Prior art: how torch/_inductor handles this case**

Inductor doesn't need a special "epilogue" mechanism for this shape at all — it falls out of two independent design choices composing, neither of which was built for RMSNorm specifically:

1. `Reduction` (`torch/_inductor/ir.py:1400`) is a plain `Loops` IR node, structurally identical to `Pointwise`. A later pointwise op that reads *both* the reduction's output buffer and the original input tensor `x` is just an ordinary node with two read deps — `x` is a separate, already-materialized buffer (a graph input or earlier-computed value), not something the reduction "hands off" specially. There is no dedicated "two-role-input" case to detect at the representation level.
2. The scheduler's generic vertical-fusion check, `Scheduler.can_fuse_vertical` (`torch/_inductor/scheduler.py:8469-8540`), fuses producer -> consumer whenever the consumer's unmet reads either match a producer's write or are already satisfiable by nodes scheduled earlier — which `x` trivially is. No fan-in-specific logic needed (see also the comment on teenygrad-1bf.2, which uses the same mechanism).

Whether the fused (reduction + epilogue) region becomes **one kernel launch** rather than two is a separate, later decision: `TritonKernel.should_use_persistent_reduction()` (`torch/_inductor/codegen/triton.py:3759`, invoked from `torch/_inductor/codegen/simd.py:560-562`). When the reduction axis fits in a single block (no `R_BLOCK` loop needed), `persistent_reduction=True` is set and the reduction result stays in registers — the epilogue's `tl.store` can then read both the register-resident reduced value and a fresh `tl.load` of `x` in the *same* kernel body, no round trip through global memory.

Directly relevant to this issue's acceptance criteria:
- **"How does region-identification recognize this two-role-input shape distinctly from case 2/case 4?"** — inductor's answer is that it doesn't need to; the same fusion-legality check (vertical fusion via read/write dependency matching) handles case 2 (fan-in), case 4 (reduction-terminated), and this case (reduction + epilogue reading the pre-reduction input) uniformly. If this design can unify its region-identification logic the same way, that's evidence it doesn't need a bespoke third detector — the retiling answer from case 4 (teenygrad-1bf.4: reduction's tiling is authoritative, producer/epilogue members must sub-tile into it) applies unchanged, because inductor doesn't distinguish "epilogue reads x directly" from "any other consumer of x" for tiling-compatibility purposes.
- The existing `RmsNormForward` reference-kernel plan in this issue's acceptance criteria is a good idea regardless — inductor's generated RMSNorm-shaped fusions are still checked against eager numerics/perf via its normal test suite, same idea.

title: fusion case 6: multi-reduction / softmax-shaped regions
description:
## Scope

Case 6 of teenygrad-1bf's fusion-case taxonomy: multi-reduction / softmax-
shaped regions. `Mul→Max→Sub→Exp→Sum` (or `Op::LogSoftmax`,
`Op::SoftmaxCrossEntropyLoss`) has two *sequential*, dependent reduction
passes over the same axis (max, then sum), each needing the completed result
of the previous pass before starting. Cannot collapse into one single-pass
generic region.

The Hexagon-MLIR paper (arXiv:2602.19762, cited in the parent spec) hits the
identical wall: "softmax, prefix-sum, TopK etc need other control-flow ops
along with linalg.generic to make them representable" — i.e. this genuinely
needs a staged two-phase kernel body (compute+store row max, barrier/re-read,
compute exp-sum, barrier, compute output), not a trick that avoids the second
pass.

## Acceptance Criteria

A written decision covering:

- Whether v1 handles this case at all, or explicitly defers it (most likely
  outcome given cases 4/6 are the hardest in the taxonomy — state this
  explicitly rather than leaving it ambiguous).
- The existing hand-written `SoftmaxForward`/`LogSoftmaxForward` kernels
  (`kernels/teeny-kernels/src/nn/activation/softmax.rs` and
  `.../activation/extra.rs`) as the reference for what a generated,
  general-purpose two-phase fused kernel would need to reproduce.
- How this depends on cases 4 and 5 (teenygrad-1bf.4, teenygrad-1bf.5) being
  resolved first, since it's a composition of two reduction-shaped regions
  chained together.

## References

Parent: teenygrad-1bf. Depends conceptually on teenygrad-1bf.4 and
teenygrad-1bf.5.
acceptance_criteria: Written decision on: (1) whether v1 handles this case or explicitly defers it, (2) SoftmaxForward/LogSoftmaxForward as the reference for a two-phase generated kernel, (3) explicit dependency on cases 4 and 5 being resolved first. No code changes required.
delete_reason: superseded: re-created with Anduin + Tile/shared-memory composition design (teenygrad-3w0 follow-on)

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Prior art: how torch/_inductor handles this case**

This is the one case where inductor's answer is stronger than what this issue's framing assumes is necessary — it has a genuine single-kernel, single-pass fusion for softmax-shaped regions via **online softmax**, not just "accept the second reduction as a second pass" or "accept two kernel launches."

- A post-grad FX pass, `prepare_softmax_pattern`/`prepare_softmax_replacement` (`torch/_inductor/fx_passes/post_grad.py:490-508`, registered at `post_grad.py:875-884`), pattern-matches the eager `amax -> sub -> exp -> sum` shape and rewrites it to `inductor_prims.prepare_softmax_online` (`torch/_inductor/inductor_prims.py:260-262`), gated by `prepare_softmax_extra_check` (`post_grad.py:511-520`: requires CUDA/XPU + Triton backend + `config.online_softmax`).
- That prim lowers (`torch/_inductor/lowering.py:9592-9615`) to `OnlineSoftmaxReduction.create` (`ir.py:2576-2610`, a `MultiOutputReduction` subclass, `reduction_type="online_softmax_reduce"`) — but **only when the reduction is large enough to be worth it** (`rnumel >= config.unroll_reductions_threshold`, `lowering.py:9604-9610`); below that it falls back to the naive two-op form inline (`lowering.py:9611-9615`), since online softmax's running-rescale bookkeeping has its own overhead that isn't worth it for small reductions.
- At codegen time this becomes a real running-max/running-sum rescale combine — `TritonKernel._online_softmax_reduce` (`codegen/triton.py:5931-5947`) emits `triton_helpers.online_softmax_reduce(...)`, which maintains a running `(max, sum)` pair and rescales the running sum whenever a new tile's max exceeds the current running max (the flash-attention trick) — all within **one kernel launch, one pass over the data**.
- Even when online softmax *isn't* used (falls under the size threshold, or `config.online_softmax` is off), inductor still keeps it to **one kernel launch**: `SIMDKernel.prepare_softmax_twopass_fallback` (`codegen/simd.py:1478-1483`) loops over the same rnumel tile twice *inside a single persistent-reduction kernel body* (`ops.reduction(..., "fmax", ...)` then `ops.reduction(..., "sum", ...)` on the shifted/exp'd values afterward) — two dependent reduction passes, but no second kernel launch, no grid-wide barrier needed because a persistent-reduction kernel already holds the whole reduction axis in registers/shared memory within one CTA.
- This is structurally similar to (but distinct from) `WelfordReduction` (`ir.py:2758`), which combines mean+M2 in a single incrementally-combinable pass — online softmax needs the running-rescale trick specifically because `sum` depends on the *final* max, which isn't known until the whole axis has been seen, so it can't be combined the way Welford's statistics can.

Directly answers this issue's core question ("whether v1 handles this case at all, or explicitly defers it... this genuinely needs a staged two-phase kernel body... not a trick that avoids the second pass"): inductor's shipped answer is that the second pass is *not* avoided architecturally, but it's also never externally visible as two kernel launches or a grid-wide barrier — both the online and non-online paths stay single-kernel by keeping the whole reduction axis resident within one CTA (persistent reduction) rather than needing any cross-CTA coordination. If this issue is scoping out a defer-vs-attempt decision, "single persistent-reduction kernel doing two sequential in-register passes over the same tile" (the non-online fallback) is a meaningfully smaller lift than full online-softmax rescaling, and might be a reasonable first target before attempting the online variant.

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Additional info: exact Myelin launch-config numbers for the softmax-shaped case, per vision-rs's TensorRT analysis**

Full writeup posted as a comment on the parent (teenygrad-1bf); summarizing what's directly relevant here.

`spinorml-1fj` (vision-rs) captured the actual generated-kernel launch config for the exact op sequence this case describes: `__myl_MulMaxrSubExpSum` (Mul->Max->Sub->Exp->Sum) runs as `block=(32,4,1)` — one warp x 4 independent rows — with 64B dynamic shared memory: a classic warp-shuffle row-reduction. Confirms TensorRT does handle this shape as a single fused kernel (not two launches), consistent with this issue's framing that it "genuinely needs a staged... kernel body."

More significant: the 11-op mega-fusion `__myl_ConcSigmAddSubConcMulConcTranSlicMaxrReshSlic` (Concat->Sigmoid->Add->Sub->Concat->Mul->Concat->Transpose->Slice->Max->Reshape->Slice, almost certainly YOLO26's detection-head decode/NMS-prep step) runs under the **exact same** `block=(32,4,1)`/64B-shared-mem structure — i.e. Myelin doesn't treat "has a reduction" as a special narrow case requiring its own kernel shape per instance; it generalizes the same warp-per-row structure to arbitrarily long surrounding chains. This is useful signal that if this case is tackled at all (rather than deferred, per this issue's own acceptance criteria noting it's likely the hardest case), a single general "reduction anchors the CTA shape, elementwise members conform" mechanism is the right target, not a special-cased "softmax kernel generator."

Separately, for comparison: torch/_inductor's approach to this exact shape (posted in an earlier comment on this issue) achieves single-kernel softmax two different ways — an online-softmax running-rescale trick when profitable, and a two-pass-inside-one-persistent-kernel fallback otherwise — neither of which needs Myelin's warp-per-row/shared-memory staging structure, because inductor's persistent reduction already holds the whole axis in registers within one CTA before the second pass even starts. Worth weighing both reference designs (Myelin's warp-shuffle two-phase kernel vs. inductor's persistent-reduction double-pass) against teeny-kernels' existing `SoftmaxForward` implementation before deciding which shape a generated version should target.

title: fusion case 7: free reindex ops via address arithmetic (reshape/slice/concat/transpose)
description:
## Scope

Case 7 of teenygrad-1bf's fusion-case taxonomy: "free" reindex ops folded via
address arithmetic (reshape/slice/concat/transpose expressed as index math,
not a structural change to block/grid shape).

Per spinorml-1fj's nsys data (vision-rs beads project) this is legitimately
free for reshape/slice/concat (`__myl_MoveResh`, `__myl_Conc`, `__myl_SlicTran`
all keep `block=(256,1,1)`, zero shared memory) but **transpose is only free
when it doesn't touch the coalescing-sensitive dimension** — transposes that
do (`__myl_DivMulTran`, `__myl_ReshTranSlic`) show non-zero static/dynamic
shared memory (a shared-memory staging tile), even though the surrounding ops
are otherwise plain elementwise.

## Acceptance Criteria

A written decision covering:

- A concrete, mechanical rule for classifying a given transpose as "pure
  index relabeling" (free) vs. "needs a staging tile" (not free) — likely
  based on whether the permuted axes include the innermost/coalescing-
  sensitive dimension.
- Confirms that "needs a staging tile" transposes get routed through case 4's
  retiling treatment (teenygrad-1bf.4), not this case's free-fusion path —
  i.e. this subtask's output is partly "here's where this case's boundary
  actually is," not just "here's how to fuse it."
- How reshape/slice/concat index-arithmetic folding is implemented at the
  `teeny-triton` DSL level (`kernels/teeny-triton/src/triton/mod.rs`) —
  pointer offset/stride rewriting into the fused kernel's addressing, not
  literal source concatenation.

## References

Parent: teenygrad-1bf. Boundary case with teenygrad-1bf.4 (reduction-
terminated regions) for the "needs staging tile" transpose sub-case.
acceptance_criteria: Written decision on: (1) a mechanical rule classifying a transpose as free (index relabeling) vs. needs-staging-tile, (2) confirmation that needs-staging-tile transposes route through case 4's retiling path, (3) how reshape/slice/concat folding is implemented at the teeny-triton DSL level. No code changes required.
delete_reason: superseded: re-created with Anduin + Tile/shared-memory composition design (teenygrad-3w0 follow-on)

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Prior art: how torch/_inductor handles this case**

Inductor's answer here is structurally flatter than this issue's proposed "free vs. needs-a-staging-tile" split for transpose — worth flagging since it suggests the boundary this issue is trying to draw may not need to exist at the fusion-legality level at all.

- Reshape/slice/concat/transpose never get their own kernel. `View.create` (`torch/_inductor/ir.py:3900-4010`) and `PermuteView.create` (`ir.py:3705-3728`) both try first to express the op as a pure stride/offset relabeling: if the input already has a concrete `storage`/`layout`, they synthesize a `ReinterpretView` (`ir.py:4179`) wrapping a `FixedLayout` (`ir.py:4848`) with recomputed `size`/`stride`/`offset` — zero codegen, just different index arithmetic baked into downstream loads.
- `PermuteView.create` (transpose) does this **unconditionally** whenever `is_storage_and_layout(x)` is true (`ir.py:3716-3726`) — there is no "needs a staging tile" branch in `ir.py` at all. A transpose is always structurally free at the IR/fusion-legality level, full stop.
- The coalescing-sensitivity concern this issue raises shows up **downstream**, in Triton codegen's tiling *choice*, never in whether fusion happens. `tiling_utils.py`'s `_analyze_memory_coalescing` (`tiling_utils.py:729-847`) walks the fused region's read/write index expressions, finds which loop variable each memory access coalesces on (`find_coalesced_var`, `tiling_utils.py:197`), and scores uncoalesced accesses so the tiling chooser can pick a 2D block tiling that makes a badly-coalesced transpose access pattern coalesced — a *block-shape* decision, not a "materialize to shared memory" decision. Inductor has no shared-memory-staging mechanism for elementwise/transpose fusion at all (that concept exists only inside the separate GEMM/conv template family — see the comment on teenygrad-1bf.8).

Relevant to this issue's acceptance criteria: inductor's precedent argues against building a mechanical "does this transpose touch the coalescing-sensitive dim -> route to case 4's retiling" rule as a fuse/don't-fuse gate. Instead, fuse unconditionally (transpose is always free at the legality level, same as reshape/slice/concat), and let a *separate*, later tiling-selection pass decide the fused region's block shape to keep the access pattern coalesced — i.e. push the coalescing concern out of the fusability decision entirely and into whatever this design's block()/grid() materialization step ends up being (see the teenygrad-1bf.4 comment's note on inductor's split between fusability-decided-at-scheduling vs. launch-config-decided-at-codegen). This would mean this case doesn't need its own boundary with case 4 at all — it can stay a pure index-arithmetic fold unconditionally, with any performance cost showing up only in tiling quality, not correctness.

For the second acceptance-criteria point (implementing the fold at the `teeny-triton` DSL level as pointer offset/stride rewriting, not literal source concatenation): inductor's `ReinterpretView`/`FixedLayout` approach is exactly that pattern — recomputed `size`/`stride`/`offset` fields consumed by downstream index-formula generation, not a textual rewrite.

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Additional info: exact Myelin shared-memory costs for non-free transpose, per vision-rs's TensorRT analysis**

Full writeup posted as a comment on the parent (teenygrad-1bf); summarizing what's directly relevant here.

`spinorml-1fj` (vision-rs) has the exact numbers behind this issue's claim that transpose isn't always free: `__myl_DivMulTran` (4224B), `__myl_ReshTranSlic` (3208B), and `__myl_Move` (3852B) — all involving a transpose that permutes the coalescing-sensitive dimension — show non-zero static/dynamic shared memory, i.e. Myelin actually allocates a real shared-memory staging tile (the classic shared-memory-transpose pattern) for these. Purely elementwise chains with no transpose, and transposes/reshapes/slices/concats that don't touch the coalescing-sensitive dim, show zero shared memory. This is concrete evidence for this issue's proposed rule (route "needs a staging tile" transposes through case 4/teenygrad-1bf.4's retiling treatment, not this case's free-fusion path) — Myelin's own behavior draws exactly that line.

**Worth flagging a contrast with torch/_inductor here** (posted in an earlier comment on this issue): inductor's `PermuteView.create` treats transpose as *unconditionally* free at the fusion-legality/IR level (pure `ReinterpretView`, stride/offset relabeling, never a kernel or a materialize decision) — coalescing quality is handled entirely as a separate, later Triton tiling-selection pass (picking a 2D block tiling that keeps the access pattern coalesced), with no shared-memory-staging mechanism for elementwise/transpose fusion at all. That's a genuinely different design point than Myelin's: inductor pushes the cost into tiling-quality (still fused, possibly worse-coalesced), while Myelin pays an explicit shared-memory staging cost to keep the access coalesced (still fused, always well-coalesced, but non-zero shared mem). Both keep the op fused rather than treating it as a hard boundary — neither system uses the "route to retiling / different CTA structure" approach this issue's draft rule proposes.

That's worth an explicit decision in this issue's acceptance criteria: does this design want Myelin's approach (pay a shared-memory tile, stay fused, guaranteed coalesced) or inductor's (stay fused via pure index arithmetic, let a separate tiling-choice step optimize coalescing after the fact, accept it might not always achieve it)? The inductor approach is structurally simpler (no staging-tile codegen needed at all, transpose is *never* a special case at the fusion-legality level) but v1 tiling-choice logic in teeny-triton would need to exist to capture any of the coalescing benefit; the Myelin approach guarantees the win per-transpose at the cost of a genuinely new staging-tile-codegen mechanism.

title: fusion case 8: GEMM/conv epilogue fusion
description:
## Scope

Case 8 of teenygrad-1bf's fusion-case taxonomy: GEMM/conv epilogue fusion
(existing `Op::Conv2dBnSilu`, `Conv2dBnSiluGemm`, `Conv2dBnSiluTiled`;
`Linear` + bias + activation is the same shape). Different tiling paradigm
entirely — tensor-core `T::dot()`-based tile shapes (see teenygrad-3i0,
teenygrad-ejt), output-tile-per-CTA with a K-dim reduction loop, nothing like
the flat elementwise grid.

Per spinorml-1fj's finding (vision-rs beads project), even TensorRT's Myelin
never fuses *through* a conv/GEMM — only elementwise/BN-style epilogues get
absorbed into its write-back.

## Acceptance Criteria

A written decision covering:

- Explicit statement that this backend does NOT attempt to merge GEMM/conv
  main loops with the generic elementwise-fusion machinery from cases 1-7 —
  document this as a hard boundary, not an oversight.
- What epilogue-absorption into an existing GEMM/conv kernel's own write-back
  looks like as a *general* mechanism, generalizing the hand-written
  `Conv2dBnSilu*` family (`kernels/teeny-kernels/src/nn/fused/`) into something
  a fusion pass can drive automatically for other conv/GEMM + epilogue
  combinations, rather than requiring a new hand-written `Op` variant per
  pattern.
- Whether epilogue absorption reuses any of case 1's elementwise-chain
  eligibility logic (is the epilogue itself just a fusable-elementwise chain,
  now attached to a GEMM/conv tail instead of another elementwise op?).

## References

Parent: teenygrad-1bf. Related: teenygrad-3i0 (tensor-core conv kernel),
teenygrad-ejt (BlockedToMMA promotion bug) for the tensor-core tiling context
this case's epilogues attach to.
acceptance_criteria: Written decision on: (1) explicit statement that GEMM/conv main loops are never merged with the elementwise-fusion machinery, (2) a general epilogue-absorption mechanism generalizing the hand-written Conv2dBnSilu* family, (3) whether epilogue absorption reuses case 1's elementwise-chain eligibility logic. No code changes required.
notes:
## YOLO26 evidence (2026-08-11)

Traced the actual YOLO26n graph (vision-rs, yolo26::<f32>(80, Variant::N, OneToMany) at 64x64 input -- 360 nodes) to check whether case-1 pointwise fusion has any adjacencies to exploit in a real model. Findings:

- 87 Silu nodes total. Every single one is immediately preceded by BatchNorm2d and (with 2 exceptions, both feeding UpsampleNearest2d in the FPN neck) immediately followed by Conv2d. Zero Silu-Silu or Silu-<other-activation> adjacencies anywhere in the graph.
- This means case-1s PointwiseFuse mechanism (teenygrad-1bf.1) cannot fire anywhere in YOLO26 as traced -- there is no unary-to-unary chain for it to find, since BatchNorm2d sits between every Conv2d and every Silu and is not PointwiseFuse-probe-eligible.
- The actual fusable adjacency in this model is exactly this cases scope: Conv2d -> BatchNorm2d -> Silu, repeated ~87 times. This is the real kernel-launch-count win for YOLO26 (vs. cases 1-7 elementwise-chain work, which has nothing to attach to here).
- Directly relevant prior art already in teenygrad history: commit 7fe3ba144 ("refactor: drop Op::Fused and orphan Conv2dBnSilu fusion") removed an existing Conv2dBnSilu fusion. kernels/teeny-kernels/tests/test_anduin_conv_bn_silu.rs (added in 8a1b53e34, after that drop) currently only validates the *unfused* 3-kernel Conv2d/BatchNorm2d/Silu pipelines numerical correctness against PyTorch -- it looks like the scaffold this case should build on to re-add the fusion.

Found while investigating case-1 (teenygrad-1bf.1) pointwise op coverage against the actual YOLO26 model in vision-rs.
delete_reason: superseded: re-created with Anduin + Tile/shared-memory composition design (teenygrad-3w0 follow-on)

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Prior art: how torch/_inductor handles this case**

Confirms this issue's core claim (Myelin never fuses through a conv/GEMM main loop) holds for inductor too — and inductor's precedent is actually *two* separate absorption mechanisms, one on each side of the main loop, neither touching the accumulation loop itself.

**Epilogue fusion** (matches this issue's scope directly): `TritonTemplate.generate` (`torch/_inductor/select_algorithm.py:2980-3037`) accepts an `epilogue_fn` (default `identity`, `select_algorithm.py:2990`) that's called on the accumulator right before the final store — the epilogue is inlined into the template's `store_output` codegen, not emitted as a separate kernel. At the scheduler level, `BaseSchedulerNode.get_prologue_template_epilogue` (`scheduler.py:2015-2027`) splits a fused node-list into `(prologue, template_node, epilogue)` by locating the template node (`n.is_template()`); `epilogue_fuse` (`scheduler.py:3204`) wires the matched epilogue's compute into the template kernel. There's also a dedicated module family for the epilogue side specifically: `torch/_inductor/kernel/gemm_epilogue.py`, `gemm_epilogue_analysis.py`, `gemm_epilogue_codegen.py`, `gemm_epilogue_utils.py`, handling e.g. grouped M/N-axis reduction epilogues (`GemmReductionGeometry`, `gemm_epilogue.py:18-56`).

**Prologue fusion** (not asked for by this issue's current scope, but worth flagging as the symmetric case teenygrad may hit later): fusing producers into the template's *input loads* (e.g. dequant-before-matmul) is a distinct, separately-gated feature — `config.prologue_fusion` (`torch/_inductor/config.py:284-285`, via `prologue_fusion_enabled()` at `config.py:71-77`) with per-template tracking of `prologue_supported_inputs`/`prologue_loads_all_inputs` (`select_algorithm.py:688-690`, `1032`, `1238`).

In neither case does inductor fuse an arbitrary elementwise chain *into* the GEMM/conv accumulation loop (`tl.dot`) the way it fuses elementwise chains with each other in cases 1-3 — the loop body itself is never a fusion target; only the load side (prologue) and store side (epilogue) are.

Relevant to this issue's acceptance criteria:
- Confirms the "hard boundary, not an oversight" framing is correct and matches shipped practice, not just Myelin's black-box behavior.
- For "generalizing the hand-written `Conv2dBnSilu*` family into something a fusion pass can drive automatically": inductor's epilogue mechanism is exactly that generalization — a generic `epilogue_fn` hook plus a scheduler-level split (`get_prologue_template_epilogue`) that classifies fused nodes as prologue/template/epilogue by position, rather than requiring a new hand-written pattern per epilogue shape.
- "Does epilogue absorption reuse case 1's elementwise-chain eligibility logic?" — in inductor's case, yes structurally: the epilogue is whatever fusable elementwise chain would otherwise have fused with the template's output buffer under the ordinary scheduler rules; the template split just changes *where* that chain's codegen gets inlined (into the template's store) rather than requiring separate eligibility rules.
- Case 11 (dtype-promotion boundaries, teenygrad-1bf.11) connection: prologue fusion is exactly where a precision boundary is most likely to be crossed in practice (dequant-into-load), so if this design later adds a symmetric prologue mechanism, it should share whatever precision-boundary rule case 11 settles on.

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Additional info: direct empirical confirmation, per vision-rs's TensorRT analysis**

Full writeup posted as a comment on the parent (teenygrad-1bf); the specific finding for this issue.

`spinorml-1fj` (vision-rs) confirmed this issue's claim directly from the nsys trace, not by inference: every conv in the whole YOLO26n trace is its own separate `xmma_fprop_implicit_gemm` kernel — none ever appears inside a `__myl_*` fusion. Only BN/activation-style epilogues get folded in, which is exactly what vision-rs's own hand-written `conv2d_bn_silu_*` kernels already do. Conv's natural tiling (output-tile-per-CTA, K-dim reduction via shared-mem/register accumulation over many iterations) is structurally incompatible with Myelin's flat elementwise map or small warp-reduction structures, and even TensorRT's fusion compiler — a mature, heavily-optimized production JIT — doesn't attempt to cross that boundary. This is independent, first-party confirmation (not just citing Myelin's black-box behavior) that "fuse around conv, never through it" is the correct target, worth citing alongside the earlier-posted torch/_inductor comparison (which shows the same boundary, plus a second `prologue_fusion` mechanism on the load side) as two independent production systems agreeing on where this line sits.

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
Design check vs Welder (OSDI'23 Shi / osdi23-shi.pdf) for Conv2d→BN→SiLU:

Verdict: Welder's design supports this fusion; Anduin's *intended* design does too (this issue); current Anduin *implementation* does not yet.

Welder:
- Explicitly unifies register-level fusion (elementwise / Matmul+BiasAdd / Conv2D+ReLU) and shared-memory fusion into one tile-graph framework.
- Fig.5 maps Conv→ReLU at L0 (register reuse-tile) then MaxPool at L1 — Conv+BN+SiLU is the same register-epilogue shape (BN is channelwise affine on the output tile).
- Mechanism: SetConnect(edge, register) + Propagate(tile shapes) + SubGraphTiling(cost), not "concat two flat kernels".

Anduin today:
- Only source-concats kernels that share PointwiseFuseProbe (flat BLOCK_SIZE=1024). Conv/BN fail that probe → 0 pointwise_fuse on YOLO26n; only 14 TileFuse(Silu+Add).
- Welder primitives partially exist (propagate.rs, KernelTileSpec on conv2d/matmul) but are not wired into Anduin::optimize for epilogue absorption.
- Closing this issue is the path: inject BN+SiLU into conv/GEMM write-back (torch inductor epilogue_fn style), not extend PointwiseFuse concat across the conv main loop.

title: fusion case 9: hard fusion barriers — grid-wide-coordination ops (top-k, sort, NMS-prep)
description:
## Scope

Case 9 of teenygrad-1bf's fusion-case taxonomy: hard fusion barriers —
grid-wide-coordination ops. Top-k, sort/argsort, NMS-prep, nonzero, and
anything needing the *entire* grid's output (not one CTA's slice) before
proceeding.

Per spinorml-1fj's finding (vision-rs beads project), a kernel-launch boundary
is a grid-wide sync/visibility barrier that `__syncthreads()` cannot
substitute for; providing that inside a single generated kernel would need
cooperative-groups grid-sync, itself capped by SM-residency (Myelin's own
`__myl_Topk` uses `grid=(1,1,1)` specifically to sidestep this rather than
attempt a grid-sync fusion).

## Acceptance Criteria

A written decision covering:

- An explicit non-fusable-boundary op stop-list (mirroring
  `is_fusable_elementwise`'s allowlist shape but as a block-list), enumerated
  against the actual `Op` variants in `core/teeny-core/src/graph/mod.rs` that
  need whole-grid coordination.
- Where this stop-list lives relative to the fusability allowlist(s) from
  other cases — shared table, or independent check — and confirms the
  region-identification pass in every other case (1, 2, 4, etc.) consults it,
  so a legitimately-adjacent barrier op can never be silently absorbed into a
  fused region.
- This is safety-critical (a missed barrier produces a silently wrong kernel,
  not just a missed optimization) — flag it as a priority to resolve before
  other cases' passes are implemented, even though this issue itself is spec-
  only.

## References

Parent: teenygrad-1bf.
acceptance_criteria: Written decision on: (1) an explicit non-fusable-boundary op stop-list enumerated against real Op variants, (2) where this stop-list lives relative to other cases' allowlists and confirmation every region-identification pass consults it, (3) flagged as priority-to-resolve-first given a missed barrier produces a silently wrong kernel. No code changes required.
delete_reason: superseded: re-created with Anduin + Tile/shared-memory composition design (teenygrad-3w0 follow-on)

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Prior art: how torch/_inductor handles this case**

Inductor doesn't maintain a static, hand-curated stop-list of op names checked by the scheduler's fusion pass. Instead the boundary is decided per-op at *lowering* time, based on whether the op's whole working set can be proven to fit in one CTA — and then enforced structurally rather than by a name check at fusion time.

- `nonzero`/`unique_dim`/etc. are unconditionally routed to `make_fallback` (`lowering.py:3837-3846`) -> an `ir.FallbackKernel` (extern/ATen call), never a candidate for Triton fusion at all.
- `sort`/`topk`/`median`/`kthvalue`/`mode` are more nuanced: `ir.Sort` (`ir.py:3209`) is a `Loops` subclass that (per its own comment at `ir.py:3223`) "mimics reduction" and gets a real Triton-generated bitonic-sort-network kernel — but `sort_stable` (`lowering.py:8202-8249`) only takes this path when `dim_size < iinfo(idx_dtype).max` (`lowering.py:8221-8224`, int16-range by default), i.e. only when the sort axis and its index array are provably small enough to fit in registers within one block (comment at `lowering.py:8216`: "bitonic network holds all indices in-block"). Once the axis is too large, it falls back to `sort_fallback`/`aten.sort.stable` (`lowering.py:8199,8224`) — an unconditional ExternKernel. `topk` (`lowering.py:8415-8428`) defaults straight to `topk_fallback` (`lowering.py:8261`) unless `config.triton.decompose_sort_ops` is set, and even then inherits the same in-block-only size limit.
- Once an op *is* an `ir.FallbackKernel`/`ExternKernel`, the barrier enforces itself structurally: `ExternKernelSchedulerNode.get_ranges()` (`scheduler.py:2235-2242`) returns `([], [])` — an empty iteration domain — so its `.group` can never satisfy `SIMDScheduling.can_fuse`'s `numel1 == numel2 and rnumel1 == rnumel2` test (`simd.py:2143`, the same check discussed on teenygrad-1bf.1) against any real pointwise/reduction neighbor. `ExternKernelSchedulerNode.is_extern()` (`scheduler.py:2227-2228`) returns `True` unconditionally and is checked at multiple template/epilogue-fusion gates (`scheduler.py:2744-2746, 2779, 3790`).

Relevant to this issue's acceptance criteria: inductor's precedent is a *provability* test ("does this fit in one CTA, given a concrete size bound on the working axis") rather than a purely op-identity-based block-list, plus a structural trick (empty iteration domain) that makes any true ExternKernel unconditionally unfusable without a separate per-call-site name check anywhere else in the fusion pass. That said, for ops with no size-bounded in-block form at all (genuinely grid-wide top-k, NMS-prep) inductor's own fallback is effectively the static block-list this issue proposes (`FallbackKernel`/`ExternKernel`, unconditional) — so the two approaches aren't in conflict: a static stop-list (this issue's proposal) is the right default, and a size-bounded "provably fits in one CTA" escape hatch (inductor's `sort`/`topk` treatment) is a plausible later refinement for ops where that's tractable, not a replacement for the stop-list itself.

This issue's "safety-critical, priority to resolve before other cases' passes are implemented" framing is worth keeping regardless of which mechanism is chosen — inductor's own enforcement is watertight only because *every* fusion-legality check (case 1's shape/tiling check, in particular) is gated on the same `.group`/`get_ranges()` data, so there's no separate code path that could accidentally skip the check.

comments.author: Arshad Mahmood
comments.text:
**Additional info: exact Myelin resource numbers for top-k, plus a notable design contrast with torch/_inductor**

Full writeup posted as a comment on the parent (teenygrad-1bf); summarizing what's directly relevant here.

`spinorml-1fj` (vision-rs) has the exact launch config for `__myl_Topk`: `grid=(1,1,1)` (a single CTA), 16.5KB static shared memory, 125 registers/thread. Confirms this issue's framing — top-k needs whole-tensor coordination, which Myelin achieves not via cooperative-groups grid-sync but by sidestepping the need for grid-wide sync entirely, cramming the whole problem into one block's shared memory and barriers. `spinorml-1fj`'s reasoning: "a kernel-launch boundary is also a grid-wide synchronization/visibility barrier, not just a per-block one... anything that can't fit in one block's worth of parallelism is forced back into separate launches regardless of source-level fusion — a hardware execution-model limit, not a compiler gap."

**Worth flagging a real design contrast for this issue's decision**, found while researching torch/_inductor's equivalent handling (posted in an earlier comment on this issue): inductor's `sort`/`topk` lowering (`torch/_inductor/lowering.py`) takes a *provability* approach rather than Myelin's single-CTA generated-kernel approach — it only generates a real Triton kernel (`ir.Sort`, a bitonic sort network) when the sort axis is provably small enough to fit within one block's registers (bounded by `iinfo(idx_dtype).max`, int16-range by default); above that bound it falls back to an ExternKernel (plain ATen call) unconditionally. Myelin's `__myl_Topk` with 125 registers/thread and 16.5KB shared memory suggests it's doing something closer to inductor's in-block path (single CTA, real generated kernel) for whatever k/tensor sizes YOLO26n's detection head uses — but the *general* question of what happens once the problem doesn't fit in one CTA's resources is answered identically by both systems: fall back to a separate, non-fused kernel launch, not attempt a grid-wide-coordinated fused kernel. This is corroborating evidence (two independent production systems, not just one) for this issue's stop-list approach being correct in the general case, while the "single-CTA, size-bounded" escape hatch (inductor's exact mechanism, and plausibly what Myelin's own `__myl_Topk` numbers reflect) is a legitimate, narrower refinement worth considering if a size bound on the relevant axis is knowable at graph-construction time.

title: feat: revive FusionCore extraction, now that #[tile(...)] exists again
notes:
## The stub, and why its reason is stale

macros/.../tiled_kernel.rs says:

    // FusionCore splice-body extraction (teenygrad-3w0.9) identified its
    // eligible kernels via `#[tile(...)]`'s tile_attrs, which no longer
    // exist -- see teenygrad-1nr.1. `fusion_core()` is unconditionally
    // `None` now; nothing computes a `Some(..)` for it any more.

`#[tile(...)]`'s attrs DO exist again. teenygrad-1nr.18 revived them and the
teenygrad-1tl epic put them on 129 forward kernels. So the stated reason for the
stub no longer holds.

## It is five live test failures

tests/test_fusion_core.rs fails with "elu_forward is single-input, single-axis,
trailing-store" on all five of:

  test_elu_forward_fusion_core_captures_body_minus_trailing_store
  test_relu_forward_fusion_core_has_no_extra_params
  test_selu_forward_fusion_core_resolves_with_no_extra_params
  test_sigmoid_tanh_exp_fusion_core_resolve
  test_fused_pointwise_relu_then_silu

They .expect() a Some(FusionCore) and get the unconditional None. These are five
of the eleven pre-existing workspace failures; the other five are
`todo!("teenygrad-1nr: implement Anduin::schedule")`.

## Why it matters more than a stubbed method

FusionCore is what makes a kernel FUSABLE, as distinct from schedulable. Its own
module doc: "input_ident is the name the auto-prelude binds the loaded input
tensor to". The auto-prelude runs only for In<Tile<..>> parameters, so:

  - a tile_spec lets `propagate` decide WHAT tile a node needs -- route 2 is
    enough for that, and resolve_inputs never looks at a parameter's type;
  - FusionCore is what lets anduin EMIT ONE KERNEL for several nodes, by
    splicing their bodies.

That is teenygrad-1nr.1's "composing Tile functions rather than
pointer-in/pointer-out kernels". Without it a fused group can be chosen and not
generated.

## Eligibility, which is the real work

The original extraction was "only available for single-input, single-axis
#[tile(...)] kernels whose hand-written body ends in a plain T::store(...)".
Two of those three conditions have moved:

  - "single-axis" is now one case among N (teenygrad-1nr.18.1/.18.5);
  - a kernel using #[tile_loop(generate)] has NO author-written trailing store
    at all -- the macro emits it -- so "body minus trailing store" has to mean
    something different for those. conv2d_forward is the example: its whole body
    is `acc = acc + x * w;`.

So this is not simply un-stubbing: it needs a decision on what a fusion core IS
for a generated-loop kernel. Worth doing against the five tests above, which
still describe the single-axis elementwise case the mechanism was built for.
close_reason: Anduin fusion work discontinued; closed with the Anduin-related issues
